Q: How can I create a self-signed certificate for 'localhost'? A:

These are the OpenSSL commands need to generate SSL keys and certificates.

1. openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -out rootCA.key -aes256 -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:4096
2. openssl req -x509 -new -key rootCA.key -sha256 -days 3650 -out rootCA.pem -config openssl.cnf -extensions v3_ca
3. openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -out server.key -aes256 -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048
4. openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr -config openssl.cnf -extensions v3_req
5. openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA rootCA.pem -CAkey rootCA.key -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 3650 -sha256 -extfile openssl.cnf -extensions v3_req
6. openssl pkcs12 -export -out server.pfx -inkey server.key -in server.crt -certfile rootCA.pem

The configuration file "openssl.cnf" used here is following:

[req]
default_bits       = 2048
default_md         = sha256
default_keyfile    = privkey.pem
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
x509_extensions    = v3_ca
string_mask        = utf8only

[req_distinguished_name]
countryName                     = PK
countryName_default             = PK
stateOrProvinceName             = SND
stateOrProvinceName_default     = SND
localityName                    = KHI
localityName_default            = KHI
organizationName                = MyOrg
organizationName_default        = MyOrg
organizationalUnitName          = RnD
commonName                      = CertificateNameToDisplay
commonName_max                  = 64

[v3_ca]
subjectKeyIdentifier = hash
authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always,issuer
basicConstraints = critical, CA:true
keyUsage = critical, cRLSign, keyCertSign

[v3_req]
basicConstraints = CA:FALSE
keyUsage = nonRepudiation, digitalSignature, keyEncipherment
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[alt_names]
DNS.1 = localhost

Check the last DNS line for "localhost". And be remember you password provided in step 1 & 6.

it’s not necessary to use the same password everywhere (although it will work)

  • Each password protects a different file/step:

    1. rootCA.key → Root private key

    2. server.key → Server private key

    3. server.pfx → Exported PKCS#12 file

Q: NestJS authorization A:

yes — you should pass the actual instance to CASL, not just the subject type.

The docs show simple examples, but CASL is designed to evaluate real objects.

Recommended pattern (scalable)

  1. Define ability with conditions
can(Action.Delete, Post, { authorId: user.id });
  1. In your guard, fetch the entity first, then check:
const post = await this.postsService.findById(params.id);

if (!this.ability.can(Action.Delete, post)) {
  throw new ForbiddenException();
}

CASL will automatically evaluate the condition (authorId === user.id) against the instance.

Why this is better than one guard per endpoint

  • Ability rules stay centralized

  • Business logic stays in CASL

  • Guard stays generic

  • Scales well as rules grow

If needed, you can create a reusable helper like:

checkAbility(action: Action, subject: AnyClass, instance: any)

But the key idea is:

Define conditional rules in CASL, fetch the entity in the guard, and pass the instance to ability.can().

That’s the intended and clean approach.
